This Lumen colocation facility is located at 2667 River Road, St. George, UT 84790, in Washington County; Lumen does not publish individual building addresses or specs on its own site for any of its 175-plus North American colocation sites. Lumen Technologies, formerly CenturyLink (renamed Lumen on September 14, 2020, with its stock ticker changing from CTL to LUMN on September 18, 2020) and built in part on CenturyLink's November 1, 2017 acquisition of Level 3 Communications, operates this facility as part of a network-centric edge colocation product rather than a wholesale hyperscale campus. Lumen's own colocation data sheet states more than 175 carrier-neutral data centers across more than 60 North American markets, offering cabinet power in the 3 to 15 kilowatt range described as varying by site; unlike the wholesale operators tracked elsewhere in this registry, Lumen does not disclose per-building square footage or total MW capacity for any of its sites.

Utah has drawn data center investment for years under its Enterprise Zone property tax abatement program, similar to the incentive structures used in other Western states tracked in this registry; St. George and southern Utah's Washington County sit outside the state's denser Salt Lake City data center corridor, giving this facility a smaller, more edge-oriented role than the wholesale campuses further north. Utah lawmakers introduced a 2026 bill requiring large water users, including data centers, to disclose their water consumption publicly, reflecting growing scrutiny of the sector's resource footprint in one of the country's most water-constrained states even as the state continues courting data center investment through its tax incentive programs.

St. George anchors a fast-growing corner of southern Utah; its data center presence is modest compared to the Salt Lake City corridor tracked elsewhere in this registry, reflecting the smaller population base and less-developed fiber and power infrastructure of Washington County relative to the Wasatch Front.

reading.body:
Lumen Technologies operates this carrier-neutral colocation facility in St. George as part of a network-oriented edge product, not as a wholesale hyperscale campus. Lumen does not publish individual facility capacity, square footage, or year-built data for any of its 175-plus North American sites; only a general cabinet power range of 3 to 15 kilowatts per cabinet applies across the fleet. Without published IT load figures, the campus cannot be positioned in the AI scaling conversation.

Southern Utah's Washington County sits outside the denser Salt Lake City data center corridor and reflects smaller population density, less-developed fiber infrastructure, and lower power availability than the Wasatch Front. St. George's modest data center presence and edge-oriented market role mean this facility is built to serve regional latency-sensitive tenants rather than large, compute-dense workloads. Lumen's cabinet-based pricing model and distributed network strategy differ fundamentally from the wholesale megawatt sales model that dominates AI infrastructure.

Utah has drawn data center investment through Enterprise Zone property tax abatement and continues recruiting operators, yet a 2026 state bill requiring large water users to disclose consumption reflects growing scrutiny of the sector's resource footprint in a water-constrained state. Of 21 mapped facilities statewide, only 9 publish megawatt figures; the state's published total is 52.18 MW. This facility cannot be ranked meaningfully without published capacity, making it immeasurable against both hyperscale AI campuses and Utah's known infrastructure base.
